clinicalPearls: Rare monogenic, autosomal recessive cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in EMP2 (epithelial membrane protein 2).
EMP2 is a tetraspan membrane protein of the GAS3/PMP22 family that regulates caveolae and caveolin-1 trafficking; it is expressed in podocytes and glomerular endothelium.
Typically presents in early childhood with oedema, heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia, often in a consanguineous or familial setting.
Clinical behaviour is variable: both steroid-sensitive and steroid-resistant phenotypes have been described, and some children show spontaneous or relapsing-remitting courses.
Renal histology most often shows minimal-change disease or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis rather than a specific diagnostic lesion.
Should be considered when a targeted genetic panel is indicated: young age of onset, family history, consanguinity, or atypical response to immunosuppression.
A confirmed genetic (podocyte-gene) diagnosis reshapes management, generally arguing against escalating immunosuppression and predicting low risk of disease recurrence after transplantation.
Distinguished from acquired immune-mediated nephrotic syndrome only by genetic testing; light microscopy alone cannot make the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: EMP2 encodes a small four-transmembrane-domain glycoprotein belonging to the growth-arrest-specific 3 (GAS3)/peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) family. These proteins partition into cholesterol-rich lipid rafts and caveolae, where EMP2 governs the surface trafficking and abundance of caveolin-1 and of several partner membrane receptors and adhesion molecules. Within the glomerulus EMP2 is expressed in podocytes and glomerular endothelial cells, compartments whose integrity depends on tightly regulated caveolar membrane organisation. Biallelic loss-of-function variants are thought to disrupt caveolae-dependent membrane dynamics and mechanotransduction at the filtration barrier, impairing podocyte foot-process architecture and slit-diaphragm signalling. The resulting breakdown of glomerular permselectivity produces the massive albuminuria and hypoalbuminaemia of the nephrotic state. Because the defect is intrinsic to the filtration barrier rather than driven by a circulating immune factor, the disorder behaves as a structural podocytopathy, which helps explain its variable and often immunotherapy-independent course.
additionalDifferentials: Other monogenic podocytopathies (NPHS1/nephrin, NPHS2/podocin, PLCE1, WT1-related disease)
Congenital and infantile nephrotic syndrome of other genetic causes
Secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (adaptive, viral, drug-related)
Syndromic nephrotic syndrome with extrarenal features
additionalInvestigations: Targeted next-generation-sequencing podocyte-gene panel or exome sequencing with EMP2 coverage
Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
Quantification of proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio) and serum albumin
Family segregation and parental carrier testing
Screening for secondary and infective causes before ascribing to a genetic cause
Assessment of thromboembolic and infection risk associated with the nephrotic state
Baseline renal function and growth/developmental assessment
redFlags: Steroid resistance or progressive decline in kidney function
Thromboembolic complications of the nephrotic state
Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca and effusions
Serious infection in an immunosuppressed or hypogammaglobulinaemic child
Rapidly worsening oedema with haemodynamic compromise
reference.prognosis: The course is heterogeneous, ranging from responsive or self-limiting disease to steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome that progresses to kidney failure. Establishing a genetic diagnosis clarifies prognosis, limits futile immunosuppression and supports favourable counselling regarding post-transplant recurrence.
pitfalls: Assuming all childhood nephrotic syndrome is immune-mediated and treatable with immunosuppression
Failing to pursue genetic testing in familial, consanguineous or steroid-resistant presentations
Prolonging or escalating immunosuppression once a monogenic cause is confirmed
Overlooking family counselling and cascade carrier testing
Attributing a non-specific minimal-change or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis biopsy to acquired disease without genetic correlation
references: Reference text on the genetics of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome
Clinical practice guidance on glomerular disease
management: Establishing the genetic diagnosis to guide therapy and limit futile immunosuppression, given the variable steroid responsiveness
A trial of corticosteroids where clinically appropriate since steroid-sensitive phenotypes occur, with calcineurin inhibitors in steroid-resistant disease under specialist guidance
Supportive nephrotic-syndrome care with dietary sodium restriction, diuretics for oedema and renin-angiotensin blockade to reduce proteinuria
Thromboprophylaxis and infection vigilance with appropriate vaccination given the hypercoagulable, immunocompromised nephrotic state
Monitoring of proteinuria, serum albumin and renal function with surveillance for progression to kidney failure
Renal replacement planning with dialysis or transplantation in progressive disease, with reassurance regarding the low post-transplant recurrence of monogenic disease
Paediatric nephrology referral and multidisciplinary care
Genetic counselling with parental carrier testing and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
